stories.headline: US Fed keeps interest rates the same, but two officials wanted a rise
stories.dek: The central bank held its key rate at 3.75%–4%. Two members voted for a hike because prices are still rising too fast.
stories.caveman: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is America's central bank. It sets a key interest rate, which changes how expensive it is to borrow money for homes, cars and businesses. On Wednesday it kept the rate at 3.75% to 4%. Most members agreed, but two of them, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, voted 'no' because they wanted to raise the rate. Prices in the US are still climbing faster than the Fed's 2% target, partly because oil prices jumped during the US war with Iran. Raising rates can cool prices down, but it can also slow the economy and cost jobs. Kevin Warsh now leads the Fed. The decision came less than a week before the US midterm elections on Nov. 3.
stories.why_it_matters: US interest rates move money around the whole world, including Taiwan's stock market and the Taiwan dollar. Two votes for a hike show the Fed may raise rates soon, which would make borrowing more expensive.
stories.camps: Rate-hike side: inflation is sticking around, so the Fed must act before it gets worse. Hold side: the economy is wobbly and oil is a supply problem that higher rates can't fix. Political angle: President Trump wants low rates, and some worry about pressure on the Fed's independence close to an election.
stories.image_alt: A Federal Reserve official speaks at a press briefing

The price of borrowing money, shown as a percentage per year.
When prices in general keep going up, so money buys less.
When a member votes against the group's decision.

stories.headline: UK Budget: £100 energy help for many homes, bigger tax on banks
stories.dek: Chancellor John Healey's first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham also raises the minimum wage by 3.9%.
stories.caveman: A 'Budget' is the UK government's yearly plan for taxes and spending. Chancellor John Healey (the finance minister) gave his first one on Wednesday. Big points: households in council-tax bands A to D, the cheaper homes, will get a £100 payment to help with energy bills. A special tax on bank profits goes up from 3% to 6%. The national minimum wage goes up by 3.9%. A cut to fuel duty (the tax on petrol and diesel) is kept going longer. Energy bills are high in Britain, and some forecasts say they could jump by over £400 in January.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how governments are trying to help people with high energy costs, and who they ask to pay for it. Here, the government chose banks.
stories.camps: Supporters: help goes to people on lower incomes, and banks made big profits from high interest rates, so they can pay more. Critics on the right: higher bank taxes could hurt investment and the City of London. Some on the left: £100 is small next to real energy bills; they want deeper changes.
stories.image_alt: Chancellor John Healey presents the Budget in the House of Commons

terms.explain: The government's yearly plan for taxes and spending.
The UK's finance minister, in charge of the Treasury.
A group that UK homes are put in by value; band A is the cheapest.
The lowest hourly pay employers are legally allowed to pay.

stories.headline: Alphabet shares fall about 10% as Google spends huge sums on AI
stories.dek: Google's parent spent more cash than it brought in, and says it will spend over $300bn on AI building next year.
stories.caveman: Alphabet owns Google. It reported results for July–September. Its cloud business made $30.7bn in sales, which is strong. But investors were worried about spending. Alphabet spent $51.36bn on 'capex' (big things like data centres and chips) in just three months, so its free cash flow turned negative: about minus $9.07bn. That means more money went out than came in. It also said its capex in 2027 will be more than $300bn, and its long-term debt has grown to $125.1bn. The share price fell around 10%.
stories.why_it_matters: Big tech firms are borrowing and spending record amounts on AI. If the bet pays off, they win big; if not, investors, workers and the wider economy could get hurt. Many of these data centres use chips made in Taiwan.
stories.camps: Bulls: AI cloud demand is real and growing, so spending now means profits later. Bears: spending is growing faster than income, and more debt makes it risky. Others: the AI building boom raises electricity use and local pushback against data centres.
stories.image_alt: A Google sign outside an office building

terms.explain: Capital expenditure: money spent on long-lasting things like buildings, machines and data centres.
Cash left after a company pays to run the business and invest. Negative means it spent more than it made.
Money a company borrowed that it must repay after more than one year.
Renting out computing power and storage over the internet.

stories.headline: Oil stays above $100 on fears the US could hit Iran after the midterms
stories.dek: Brent crude was about $115 a barrel after reports the US told Gulf allies to get ready.
stories.caveman: Oil prices have been very high because of the war involving the US and Iran. On Wednesday, Brent crude (a world price) was about $115.32 a barrel and US WTI oil about $102.78. Traders were nervous after reports that the US told Gulf states to prepare for possible strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections. Iran-allied Houthi militants also said they fired a ballistic missile at Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery. The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route where lots of the world's oil passes, is a major worry.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil price affects petrol, electricity, airline tickets and the price of almost everything that is shipped. Taiwan imports nearly all its energy, so this hits Taiwan too.
stories.camps: Hawks: say pressure on Iran is needed for security. Critics and anti-war voices: another round of strikes could widen the war and push prices even higher. Economists: high oil feeds inflation, making it harder for central banks to cut interest rates.
stories.image_alt: Oil pumpjacks in a field

stories.headline: Apple shows its first touchscreen MacBook Pro
stories.dek: After years of saying no, Apple adds a touch screen to its pro laptops. They go on sale Nov. 6 from $2,899.
stories.caveman: For a long time Apple said laptops should not have touch screens; that's what the iPad was for. Now it has changed its mind. The new MacBook Pro has a touch screen Apple calls 'ProLED XDR' and runs on new M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. It goes on sale Nov. 6 and starts at $2,899 for the smaller model and $3,399 for the bigger one. Apple's CEO is now John Ternus. The launch comes at a hard time: overall PC shipments fell 20% in the third quarter (IDC data), and analysts say an AI-driven shortage of memory chips has pushed laptop prices up.
stories.why_it_matters: Apple's choices shape how the whole industry designs gadgets. Many of the parts and chips inside Macs are made in Taiwan.
stories.camps: Fans: touch makes the Mac easier and more flexible. Skeptics: it's very expensive and may blur the line with the iPad. Industry watchers: with PC sales falling, a big new feature may be what Apple needs to get people to upgrade.
stories.image_alt: People try out new Apple laptops

terms.explain: A screen you can control by touching it with your fingers.
Apple's own computer chips; Pro and Max are the more powerful versions.
The number of personal computers sent out to stores and buyers.
Chief executive officer, the top boss of a company.

stories.headline: US Justice Department looks into Nvidia's $12.9bn Hugging Face deal
stories.dek: Officials are asking whether the AI chip giant buying a popular open AI platform could hurt competition.
stories.caveman: Nvidia makes most of the chips that power AI and is one of the world's most valuable companies. It agreed to spend $12.9bn on Hugging Face, a popular website where people share free 'open' AI models and tools. Now the US Department of Justice (DOJ) is asking questions about the deal. Its job includes stopping deals that give one company too much power and hurt competition. A probe does not mean the deal will be blocked, but it can slow it down or force changes.
stories.why_it_matters: Hugging Face is a key meeting place for open AI. If one giant owns both the chips and the place where many AI models are shared, it could shape who gets to build AI and on what terms.
stories.camps: Nvidia's side: the deal helps developers and open AI grow. Competition watchdogs: Nvidia is already very powerful, and buying a key hub could squeeze rivals. Open-source community: worried about whether the platform will stay neutral.
stories.image_alt: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

terms.explain: The US government department in charge of law enforcement and enforcing competition laws.
Laws that stop companies from getting too much market power.
Software or AI models that anyone can see, use and change for free.
An official investigation.

stories.headline: Musk's xAI offers to buy homes near its noisy power plant, if owners skip a lawsuit
stories.dek: In Southaven, Mississippi, neighbours say the AI site is loud and polluting. The company's offer comes with a catch.
stories.caveman: xAI is Elon Musk's AI company. It runs giant data centres in the Memphis area, including in Southaven, Mississippi, using dozens of gas turbines (69, according to the Guardian) to make power. Neighbours say the noise never stops and worry about pollution; some have joined a lawsuit. Now agents working for xAI are going door to door offering to buy houses, on one condition: the owners must not join a neighbour's class-action lawsuit over the noise. A realtor reportedly said the target is 418 homes, and 18 owners have already agreed. xAI denies the lawsuit's claims and says it wants to be a good neighbour. Some locals call the idea 'Elonville'.
stories.why_it_matters: AI needs huge amounts of electricity. Who pays the price, in noise, dirty air and lost homes, is a big fairness question, and it often falls on nearby neighbourhoods with little power to say no.
stories.camps: xAI's side: the data centres bring investment and jobs, and buying homes gives people a way out. Residents and environmental groups: the company is pushing people out and trying to weaken the lawsuit. Local officials: split between wanting the money and protecting residents.
stories.image_alt: Jason Haley near one of the xAI data centres close to his home in Southaven, Mississippi

terms.explain: A big building full of computers that run websites and AI.
A machine that burns natural gas to make electricity.
A case brought to court by people who say they were harmed.
Elon Musk's artificial intelligence company, maker of the Grok chatbot.

stories.headline: Hackers leak details of over 41,000 US homeland security staff
stories.dek: Activist hackers say they got in through Okta, a login company; Okta denies its systems were broken into.
stories.caveman: A hacker group calling itself the 'Department of Peace', with well-known hacker maia crimew, says it leaked personal details of more than 41,000 staff at the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS). That includes about 21,000 border agents (CBP) and about 6,600 immigration agents (ICE). The data was shared through DDoSecrets, a group that publishes leaked documents, in a release called 'Icepick'. The hackers claim they got access through Okta, a company that handles logins for many organisations. Okta says it was not hacked. ICE agents often work with their faces covered by masks and sunglasses.
stories.why_it_matters: Leaks like this raise hard questions: is exposing government agents holding power to account, or does it put people and their families in danger?
stories.camps: Supporters of the leak: ICE has been accused of harsh, secretive raids, and the public deserves to know who is doing them. Critics and the government: publishing personal details can lead to harassment and threats, and hacking is a crime. Security experts: shows how one login system can be a weak point.
stories.image_alt: US immigration agents in masks

terms.explain: Department of Homeland Security, the US agency for border, immigration and disaster security.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which arrests and deports immigrants.
Customs and Border Protection, which guards US borders and ports.

stories.headline: Israel election still undecided: Netanyahu's bloc leads but lacks a majority
stories.dek: With about 85% of votes counted, his side has 53 seats; up to 480,000 absentee ballots are still to come.
stories.caveman: Israel's parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats. To form a government, a group of parties needs 61. With about 85% of votes counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing bloc had 53 seats. A bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot had 48, and Arab-led parties 19. About 430,000 to 480,000 absentee ballots (from soldiers, diplomats and others) still need counting, so the numbers can change. Netanyahu called for 'a strong right-wing national government'. During the vote he also shared an AI-made image of Arab voters, which drew attention.
stories.why_it_matters: Who runs Israel affects the war in Gaza and the wider Middle East, which has pushed up oil prices worldwide.
stories.camps: Netanyahu's supporters: he keeps Israel strong against its enemies. Opponents: after years of war and corruption trials, it's time for change. Arab citizens: worry about being shut out and targeted by campaign messages.
stories.image_alt: Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters

terms.explain: Israel's parliament, with 120 seats.
A group of parties that work together.
A government formed by several parties together.
Votes cast by people who can't vote at their usual polling place, like soldiers.

stories.headline: Brazil's Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami and calls himself the 'true president'
stories.dek: After losing to Lula, he flew to the US with his family and repeated claims of fraud that courts have rejected.
stories.caveman: Brazil held its presidential election and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term. His rival, Flávio Bolsonaro (son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro), flew with his wife and daughters to Miami, wearing a bulletproof vest. In a letter, he called himself Brazil's 'true president', later changing it to 'leader of Brazil', and again claimed, without evidence, that there was 'electoral fraud'. Brazil's courts and even his own party have accepted the result. Brazilian papers say his family got humanitarian visas to the US; Trump said he gave him 'a pass' but won't get involved.
stories.why_it_matters: It echoes the 2022 and 2020 fights over stolen-election claims in Brazil and the US. Refusing to accept a vote weakens trust in democracy.
stories.camps: Bolsonaro and supporters: claim the vote was unfair. Brazil's courts, Congress leaders and his own party: the result is valid. Lula's camp: says he's running away from the law. US angle: critics say letting him in signals support for election denial.
stories.image_alt: Flávio Bolsonaro steps off a plane at Miami-Opa Locka airport, Florida
stories.image_credit: Photo: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: Cheating in an election, such as fake votes. Brazil's courts found no evidence of it.

stories.headline: Putin calls Elon Musk a 'real genius' and pushes Russia's own satellite internet
stories.dek: Russia wants its Rassvet network to rival Starlink, which Ukraine has relied on during the war.
stories.caveman: Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk as a 'real genius' while promoting Rassvet, Russia's plan for its own satellite internet. Musk's Starlink already has about 13,000 satellites. Ukraine has used Starlink to fight Russia's invasion, but last week Ukrainian troops had sudden Starlink problems, which Musk admitted SpaceX did on purpose. The comments come as the US and Russia seem to be getting closer: Trump recently struck a deal to import Russian diesel, waived some sanctions, and a US citizen was released from Russian custody.
stories.why_it_matters: Satellite internet has become a weapon of war. Who controls it, a country or one billionaire, matters for Ukraine and also for Taiwan, which is planning its own satellite backup.
stories.camps: Russia: wants independence from Western tech. Ukraine and allies: alarmed that one private company can switch off service in wartime. Critics in the US: warn that warmer US-Russia ties may come at Ukraine's expense.
stories.image_alt: Russian President Vladimir Putin

terms.explain: SpaceX's satellite internet service.
Russia's planned satellite internet network.
Penalties, such as trade limits, one country puts on another.
Internet sent from satellites in space instead of cables.

stories.headline: US Justice Department pressures a California election official over 'noncitizen' voters
stories.dek: A county clerk says federal officials threatened him over a list of 47 people they claim weren't citizens.
stories.caveman: In the US, local officials run elections. Keaton Denlay, the elections clerk in Butte County, California, says the federal Department of Justice threatened him after it handed over a list of 47 people it said were 'noncitizens' on voter lists. Election officials say checks like this must follow the law and real evidence, because mistakes can remove citizens' right to vote. Studies have found that voting by noncitizens is very rare. This comes just before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
stories.why_it_matters: How elections are run, and who gets removed from voter rolls, decides who can vote. Federal pressure on local officials raises worries about fair elections.
stories.camps: Trump administration: says it is protecting elections from illegal voting. Election officials and voting-rights groups: say these claims are often wrong and the pressure is meant to scare officials and voters. Neutral experts: noncitizen voting is rare, but voter rolls should be kept accurate through proper legal steps.
stories.image_alt: A man votes in Beverly Hills, California
stories.image_credit: Photo: Daniel Cole/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: A local official who manages records and, often, elections.

The US government department in charge of law enforcement.

stories.headline: HOT (with a catch): 'Sarah J. Maas, Inc.' as ACOTAR becomes a merch empire
stories.dek: Underwear, blankets, kettle corn and $700 gowns: the romantasy hit is now a big brand, and small fan sellers say they're being pushed out.
stories.caveman: Sarah J. Maas writes A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR), a hugely popular romantasy series. The sixth book came out Oct. 27, and the series has sold over 10.5 million copies in trade paperback alone. Publishers Weekly reports that, since Maas moved her licensing to the big agency IMG in 2025, ACOTAR merchandise is everywhere: an underwear line with Knix, throw blankets at Sam's Club, Target kettle corn and gowns costing over $700. But many small fan-run shops, which used to have official licences, say IMG let their licences expire and did not answer their requests. Some fans love the merch; others feel the fan spirit is turning into big business.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how a book can turn into a full brand like a movie franchise, and who wins and loses when that happens.
stories.camps: Fans who like it: more ways to enjoy the world they love. Small creators: the big brands are squeezing out the people who built the fan culture. Industry: licensing brings in money and new readers.
stories.image_alt: Mannequins wearing ACOTAR-themed underwear at the Knix launch in New York

terms.explain: Books that mix romance and fantasy.
Letting another company use your name or characters on products, for a fee.
Merchandise: products like clothes or mugs based on a brand or story.
A larger, better-quality paperback book format.

stories.headline: HOT: Anand Giridharadas' new book revisits Jordan Neely's death on the subway
stories.dek: 'Man in the Mirror' argues that both Neely and the man who choked him, Daniel Penny, felt abandoned by America.
stories.caveman: In May 2023, Jordan Neely, an unhoused Black man in a mental-health crisis, was shouting threats on a New York subway. Daniel Penny, a white former Marine, held him in a chokehold for about six minutes and Neely died. Video of it split the country. In 2024, Penny was found not guilty of criminally negligent homicide. Journalist Anand Giridharadas spent over two years reporting for his new book, Man in the Mirror: Hope, Struggle, and Belonging in an American City. He says both men felt let down by systems that should have helped them, and that social media turned real people into cartoons.
stories.why_it_matters: The case touches race, homelessness, mental health and public safety, all big debates in US cities, including in New York's politics now.
stories.camps: Neely's supporters: a Black man in crisis was treated as disposable. Penny's supporters: he stepped in when no police were there. The author's view: look past the viral video to the failures that put both men in that subway car.
stories.image_alt: Protesters rally in support of Jordan Neely in New York City in May 2023
stories.image_credit: Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images via NPR

terms.explain: Without a home; a gentler word for homeless.
Holding someone around the neck so they can't breathe well.
Found not guilty by a court.
Causing a death through extremely careless behaviour.

stories.headline: HOT: Batman legends and translated comics shine at the Harvey Awards
stories.dek: At New York Comic Con, the comics awards celebrated 40 years of 'The Dark Knight Returns' and gave new prizes for comics in translation.
stories.caveman: The Harvey Awards are big prizes in the US comics world, named after Mad magazine cartoonist Harvey Kurtzman. This year's ceremony at New York Comic Con was packed with stars. To mark 40 years since The Dark Knight Returns, all the Hall of Fame honourees were people important to Batman comics, like artist David Mazzucchelli and Jenette Kahn, who led DC Comics for over 20 years. Actor Thomas Jane won Best Digital Book for his comic The Lycan. For the first time, the night also included the Sophie Castille Awards for Comics in Translation, honouring comics from other languages.
stories.why_it_matters: Comics and graphic novels are among the fastest-growing parts of US book sales, and a translation prize helps readers discover stories from beyond America.
stories.camps: Fans: a fun celebration of comics history. Critics of the industry: superhero nostalgia still takes the spotlight from newer voices. Translation advocates: the new prize is a welcome step.
stories.image_alt: Winners pose with Harvey Awards trophies at New York Comic Con

terms.explain: US comics awards named after cartoonist Harvey Kurtzman.

stories.headline: NOT for Kushner: new book's money claims spark a political fight
stories.dek: 'Princes and Thieves' links Jared Kushner to Gulf money; he calls it 'completely insane' and threatens to sue.
stories.caveman: Jared Kushner is President Trump's son-in-law and one of his top Middle East envoys. A new book by journalist Matthew Cole, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East, came out in the US this week. It makes explosive claims linking Kushner to large bank accounts allegedly funded by Gulf states during Trump's first term. Kushner denies everything, says the author has no evidence, demanded that Vanity Fair take down its excerpt, and threatened legal action against the publisher, Simon & Schuster.
stories.why_it_matters: Books like this can push questions about money and power into public debate, but claims still need solid evidence.
stories.camps: Kushner: the claims are false and were already denied on the record. The author and publisher: stand by the reporting so far. Critics of Trump's family: want official investigations into foreign money. Neutral observers: wait to see the evidence tested.
stories.image_alt: Jared Kushner speaks at a Board of Peace session in New York
stories.image_credit: Photo: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: A person sent by a government to represent it in talks.
A short part taken from a longer book.
A claim that someone did something wrong, not yet proven.
A major US book publisher.

stories.headline: Dolores Huerta, farmworker champion who coined 'Sí, se puede', dies at 96
stories.dek: She co-founded the United Farm Workers and fought for workers, women and LGBTQ+ people into her 90s.
stories.caveman: Dolores Huerta helped start the United Farm Workers union, which fought for better pay and safer conditions for people picking fruit and vegetables in the US, many of them Latino. She created the slogan 'Sí, se puede!' ('Yes, it can be done!'), later used by Barack Obama's 2008 campaign. She kept marching and speaking about race, poverty, women's and LGBTQ+ rights well into her 90s and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. Her family said she died at home on Wednesday. Earlier this year, she revealed that union co-founder César Chávez had sexually abused her in the 1960s, a secret she kept for 60 years.
stories.why_it_matters: She is one of the most important labour and feminist leaders in US history, and showed that ordinary workers organising together can win.
stories.camps: Admirers: a hero for workers, women and immigrants. Her revelation this year also made many rethink how movements protect women inside them. Some critics on the right opposed her union and political activism.
stories.image_alt: Dolores Huerta at the California Democratic Party convention in 2025

terms.explain: A group of workers who join together to bargain for better pay and conditions.
A US union for farmworkers, founded in the 1960s.
Spanish for 'Yes, it can be done', a famous protest slogan.
The highest award a US civilian can receive.

stories.headline: Spain high-speed train crash kills at least 68
stories.dek: A train from Madrid hit another train that had stopped on the tracks; the minister blames a computer failure and human error.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday morning, a high-speed train going from Madrid to Seville crashed into another train that was standing still on the tracks, about 140km south of Madrid. At least 68 people died and dozens were hurt; several carriages fell down a slope. The stopped train, run by private company Iryo, had 147 passengers; the moving one, run by state railway Renfe, had 397. Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a computer failure stopped the first train, then a control centre in Madrid made an 'inexplicable' decision to let trains move again with no speed limits. It is Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.
stories.why_it_matters: Fast trains are usually very safe, so a crash like this raises hard questions about automated systems and human checks, lessons for every country with high-speed rail, including Taiwan.
stories.camps: Government: points to a system failure followed by human error and promises answers. Rail unions and critics: ask whether private competition and cost-cutting stretched safety. Families: want full accountability.
stories.image_alt: Train carriages after the high-speed crash in central Spain

terms.explain: Trains that run much faster than normal, often over 250km/h.
Spain's state-owned railway company.
A private rail company running high-speed trains in Spain.
A room where staff watch and direct train traffic.

stories.headline: Africa's Ebola outbreak is 'unprecedented' and could reach the UK, health chief warns
stories.dek: With about 10,000 cases and nearly 5,000 deaths, Africa CDC's leader compares it to the early days of Covid.
stories.caveman: Ebola is a dangerous disease that spreads through body fluids like blood or vomit. The current outbreak started in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and has spread to Kenya and Uganda. It has reached about 10,000 cases and almost 5,000 deaths, and for the first time three African regions are affected. Dr Jean Kaseya, head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said every country, including the UK, should get ready. He reminded people that at the start of Covid, many countries said there was no risk, then became hotspots.
stories.why_it_matters: Diseases don't stop at borders. Helping poorer countries fight outbreaks early protects everyone.
stories.camps: Health experts: rich countries should send money, vaccines and staff now, not later. Some governments: focus on border checks at home. Aid groups: cuts to global health funding have made outbreaks harder to control.
stories.image_alt: A map of countries affected by Ebola at the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control in Abuja
stories.image_credit: Photo: Sodiq Adelakun/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: A severe, often deadly virus spread through body fluids.
A sudden rise in cases of a disease in one area.
Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the African Union's public health agency.
A place where a disease is spreading fast.

stories.headline: Iran gives film-maker Jafar Panahi a new prison sentence and seizes his assets
stories.dek: The Palme d'Or winner got five years and one month in a trial he didn't attend, plus a travel ban.
stories.caveman: Jafar Panahi is one of Iran's most famous film directors. Last year he won the top prize at Cannes, the Palme d'Or, for It Was Just an Accident. Now an Iranian court has sentenced him, in absentia (without him there), to five years and one month in prison, ordered all his assets seized, banned him from travelling for two years and from social media for two years. His lawyer says the charges are unclear and they only learned of the case when his bank accounts were frozen. A friend says Panahi has not been arrested yet. Human rights groups say Iran is cracking down on artists.
stories.why_it_matters: Punishing artists is a way to scare a whole society into silence. Panahi's case is watched worldwide as a test of free expression in Iran.
stories.camps: Iran's authorities: say they are enforcing the law against 'propaganda'. Human rights groups and film-makers: say it is punishment for telling the truth in his films. Legal experts: say seizing assets without a clear legal link may break Iran's own constitution.
stories.image_alt: Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi
stories.image_credit: Photo: Carlos Álvarez/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: When a trial happens without the accused person present.
The top prize at the Cannes Film Festival.
Things a person owns that have value, like money, property or homes.
Strong government action to stop or punish something, often critics.
